A dynamic matrix lets the student decide how many rows or columns the answer
needs. This is useful when finding the size is part of the mathematics—for
example, when the dimension of a subspace is not given in advance.

{{< include _includes/input-guide-en.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Changing the matrix size"}
Use the **−** and **+** buttons beside **Rows** or **Columns** before or while
entering the matrix. Only dimensions that the exercise allows you to change are
shown. Fill every visible cell, then select **Check**.

In exercises that assess complete vectors, all cells in a row or column receive
the same color. Green means that vector is valid *and adds a new independent
direction*. A red vector may be outside the required space, zero, or redundant.
The whole answer is correct only when the submitted vectors form a complete
basis.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="For exercise authors"}
Write a resizable input as, for example,
`mat{name=Z, rows=3, cols=auto, initial-cols=1, min-cols=0, max-cols=3}`.
Dynamic matrices use `mode: custom`. The checker receives the SymPy matrix at
`response["inputs"][name]["matrix"]` and can return whole-vector assessment as
`{"assessment": {"Z": {"columns": [...]}}}` or
`{"assessment": {"R": {"rows": [...]}}}`.
:::

## Bases with an unknown number of vectors

The number of basis vectors is the dimension of the subspace, so the student
must determine both the entries and the number of vectors.

::: {#dynamic-basis-method .math-exercise-context}

To check a proposed basis:

1. Verify that every vector belongs to the required subspace.
2. Remove zero or redundant vectors; every remaining vector must add a new
   independent direction.
3. Verify that the independent vectors span the entire subspace.

:::

### Null-space basis

```{math-exercise}
#| label: dynamic-nullspace-basis
#| caption: A basis without announcing nullity
#| mode: custom
#| context: dynamic-basis-method
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       Z = response["inputs"]["Z"]["matrix"]
#|       C = Matrix([[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]])
#|       target_dim = C.cols - C.rank()
#|       accepted = []
#|       column_status = []
#|       for j in range(Z.cols):
#|           vector = Z[:, j]
#|           belongs = (
#|               Z.rows == C.cols
#|               and vector != zeros(Z.rows, 1)
#|               and C * vector == zeros(C.rows, 1)
#|           )
#|           trial = accepted + [vector]
#|           adds_direction = belongs and Matrix.hstack(*trial).rank() == len(trial)
#|           column_status.append(adds_direction)
#|           if adds_direction:
#|               accepted.append(vector)
#|       coverage = min(len(accepted), target_dim) / target_dim
#|       precision = len(accepted) / Z.cols if Z.cols else 0
#|       score = coverage * precision
#|       feedback = "" if score == 1 else (
#|           "This null space is not trivial; add basis vectors." if Z.cols == 0
#|           else "A red column is zero, outside the null space, or redundant. Keep enough independent columns to span the null space."
#|       )
#|       return {
#|           "score": score,
#|           "feedback": feedback,
#|           "assessment": {"Z": {"columns": column_status}}
#|       }

Give a basis for the null space of
$C=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\end{bmatrix}$.
Enter one basis vector per column of $Z$. Use the column controls to decide how
many vectors are needed:

$Z=$ mat{name=Z, rows=3, cols=auto, initial-cols=1, min-cols=0, max-cols=3}
```

### Column-space basis

```{math-exercise}
#| label: dynamic-column-space-basis
#| caption: Compute a basis for a column space
#| mode: custom
#| context: dynamic-basis-method
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       B = response["inputs"]["B"]["matrix"]
#|       A = Matrix([[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 1], [1, 3, 1]])
#|       target_dim = A.rank()
#|       accepted = []
#|       column_status = []
#|       for j in range(B.cols):
#|           vector = B[:, j]
#|           belongs = (
#|               B.rows == A.rows
#|               and vector != zeros(B.rows, 1)
#|               and A.row_join(vector).rank() == A.rank()
#|           )
#|           trial = accepted + [vector]
#|           adds_direction = belongs and Matrix.hstack(*trial).rank() == len(trial)
#|           column_status.append(adds_direction)
#|           if adds_direction:
#|               accepted.append(vector)
#|       coverage = min(len(accepted), target_dim) / target_dim
#|       precision = len(accepted) / B.cols if B.cols else 0
#|       score = coverage * precision
#|       feedback = "" if score == 1 else (
#|           "This column space is not trivial; add basis vectors." if B.cols == 0
#|           else "A red column is zero, outside the column space, or redundant. Keep only enough independent columns to span the space."
#|       )
#|       return {
#|           "score": score,
#|           "feedback": feedback,
#|           "assessment": {"B": {"columns": column_status}}
#|       }

Compute a basis for the column space of
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&1\\1&3&1\end{bmatrix}$.
Your basis may use columns of $A$ or any other vectors in its column space.
Enter one basis vector per column of $B$:

$B=$ mat{name=B, rows=3, cols=auto, initial-cols=1, min-cols=0, max-cols=3}
```

### Row-space basis

```{math-exercise}
#| label: dynamic-row-space-basis
#| caption: Compute a basis using row vectors
#| mode: custom
#| context: dynamic-basis-method
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       R = response["inputs"]["R"]["matrix"]
#|       A = Matrix([[1, 0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 1, 1], [1, 1, 2, 3]])
#|       target_dim = A.rank()
#|       accepted = []
#|       row_status = []
#|       for i in range(R.rows):
#|           vector = R[i, :]
#|           belongs = (
#|               R.cols == A.cols
#|               and vector != zeros(1, R.cols)
#|               and A.col_join(vector).rank() == A.rank()
#|           )
#|           trial = accepted + [vector]
#|           adds_direction = belongs and Matrix.vstack(*trial).rank() == len(trial)
#|           row_status.append(adds_direction)
#|           if adds_direction:
#|               accepted.append(vector)
#|       coverage = min(len(accepted), target_dim) / target_dim
#|       precision = len(accepted) / R.rows if R.rows else 0
#|       score = coverage * precision
#|       feedback = "" if score == 1 else (
#|           "This row space is not trivial; add basis vectors." if R.rows == 0
#|           else "A red row is zero, outside the row space, or redundant. Keep only enough independent rows to span the space."
#|       )
#|       return {
#|           "score": score,
#|           "feedback": feedback,
#|           "assessment": {"R": {"rows": row_status}}
#|       }

Compute a basis for the row space of
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1&2\\0&1&1&1\\1&1&2&3\end{bmatrix}$.
Enter one basis vector per row of $R$, and use the row controls to choose how
many vectors are needed:

$R=$ mat{name=R, rows=auto, cols=4, initial-rows=1, min-rows=0, max-rows=3}
```

## Matrix size as part of the problem

These exercises use adjustable dimensions for reasons other than choosing a
basis. Read the task before changing the initial size.

### Hessian with three variables

```{math-exercise}
#| label: dynamic-hessian
#| caption: Build a 3 × 3 Hessian from a 2 × 2 start
#| mode: custom
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       H = response["inputs"]["H"]["matrix"]
#|       target = Matrix([[2, 1, 0], [1, 4, 1], [0, 1, 6]])
#|       shape_ok = H.shape == target.shape
#|       row_status = [
#|           shape_ok and all(simplify(H[i, j] - target[i, j]) == 0 for j in range(3))
#|           for i in range(H.rows)
#|       ]
#|       score = sum(row_status) / 3
#|       return {
#|           "score": score,
#|           "feedback": "" if score == 1 else "A Hessian has one row and one column for every variable. After fixing the size, check each second derivative.",
#|           "assessment": {"H": {"rows": row_status}}
#|       }

Find the Hessian of
$f(x,y,z)=x^2+xy+2y^2+yz+3z^2$.
There are three variables, but the input deliberately starts at $2\times2$.
First correct its size, then enter the second derivatives:

$H_f=$ mat{name=H, rows=auto, cols=auto, initial-rows=2, initial-cols=2, min-rows=1, max-rows=3, min-cols=1, max-cols=3}
```

### Adjacency matrix of a path

```{math-exercise}
#| label: dynamic-path-adjacency
#| caption: Let the matrix size choose the graph
#| mode: custom
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       P = response["inputs"]["Pth"]["matrix"]
#|       square = P.rows == P.cols
#|       target = Matrix(P.rows, P.cols, lambda i, j: int(abs(i-j) == 1)) if square else None
#|       row_status = [
#|           square and all(simplify(P[i, j] - target[i, j]) == 0 for j in range(P.cols))
#|           for i in range(P.rows)
#|       ]
#|       score = sum(row_status) / P.rows if P.rows else 0
#|       return {
#|           "score": score,
#|           "feedback": "" if score == 1 else "The matrix must be square. Put 1 exactly where consecutive vertices meet and 0 everywhere else.",
#|           "assessment": {"Pth": {"rows": row_status}}
#|       }

Choose between two and five ordered vertices. Enter the adjacency matrix of the
path $v_1-v_2-\cdots-v_n$. The number of rows and columns chooses $n$.
Consecutive vertices are joined; no other pair is joined:

$P_n=$ mat{name=Pth, rows=auto, cols=auto, initial-rows=2, initial-cols=2, min-rows=2, max-rows=5, min-cols=2, max-cols=5}
```

### A variable-length list of points

```{math-exercise}
#| label: dynamic-point-rows
#| caption: Choose how many points to submit
#| mode: custom
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       P = response["inputs"]["P"]["matrix"]
#|       seen = set()
#|       row_status = []
#|       for i in range(P.rows):
#|           point = tuple(P.row(i))
#|           valid = simplify(P[i, 1] - 2*P[i, 0]) == 0 and point not in seen
#|           row_status.append(valid)
#|           if valid:
#|               seen.add(point)
#|       score = sum(row_status) / P.rows
#|       return {
#|           "score": score,
#|           "feedback": "" if score == 1 else "Each red row must be changed: it is either off the line or duplicates an earlier point.",
#|           "assessment": {"P": {"rows": row_status}}
#|       }

Give between two and four distinct points on the line $y=2x$. Enter one point
$(x,y)$ per row. Use the row controls to choose how many points to submit:

$P=$ mat{name=P, rows=auto, cols=2, initial-rows=2, min-rows=2, max-rows=4}
```

### A non-square zero matrix

```{math-exercise}
#| label: dynamic-both-dimensions
#| caption: Choose both dimensions
#| mode: custom
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       A = response["inputs"]["A"]["matrix"]
#|       non_square = A.rows != A.cols
#|       zero = A == zeros(A.rows, A.cols)
#|       score = (int(non_square) + int(zero)) / 2
#|       return {
#|           "score": score,
#|           "feedback": "" if score == 1 else "The matrix must have different numbers of rows and columns, and every entry must be zero."
#|       }

Give any non-square zero matrix with at least one row and one column. Both its
size and its entries are part of the answer:

$A=$ mat{name=A, rows=auto, cols=auto, initial-rows=2, initial-cols=1, min-rows=1, max-rows=4, min-cols=1, max-cols=4}
```

## Empty matrix edge cases

The final two exercises test the canonical empty state. A matrix with no entries
is shown simply as **Empty matrix**, regardless of whether the last action
removed its final row or its final column. Adding a row or column restores the
other configured dimension.

### Empty basis for a trivial null space

```{math-exercise}
#| label: dynamic-zero-columns
#| caption: Remove the last basis-vector column
#| mode: custom
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       Z = response["inputs"]["Z0"]["matrix"]
#|       correct = Z.rows == 0 and Z.cols == 0
#|       return {
#|           "correct": correct,
#|           "feedback": "" if correct else "The null space contains only the zero vector, so its basis contains no vectors. Remove the remaining column."
#|       }

Give a basis for the null space of $I_2$. Because this null space is trivial,
its basis is empty. Remove the remaining column:

$Z_0=$ mat{name=Z0, rows=2, cols=auto, initial-cols=1, min-cols=0, max-cols=2}
```

### Empty state reached by removing rows

```{math-exercise}
#| label: dynamic-zero-rows
#| caption: Test restoration of a fixed column dimension
#| mode: custom
#| checker: |
#|   def check(response, symbols):
#|       T = response["inputs"]["T"]["matrix"]
#|       correct = T.rows == 0 and T.cols == 0
#|       return {
#|           "correct": correct,
#|           "feedback": "" if correct else "Remove every row to submit the empty matrix."
#|       }

Use the row control to remove the only row. After checking the empty state, add
a row again: the two configured columns should reappear.

$T=$ mat{name=T, rows=auto, cols=2, initial-rows=1, min-rows=0, max-rows=3}
```
